news.article_content_en:
The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia.

On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents.

According to officials, D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully this summer after being recruited by co-conspirators through Telegram. His alleged mission was to “carry out clandestine assignments targeting employees of a large technology and defense company with an office in Palo Alto, California”, the justice department said, without identifying the company or the alleged co-conspirators.

Bloomberg reported that the company in question was Palantir Technologies, citing an unnamed source familiar with the matter. The firm has a large office in Palo Alto.

The department added that D’iu had reportedly received instructions, equipment and financial support from the co-conspirators, who told him that his work was for “the Motherland”.

They also allegedly instructed him to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine.

The Russian embassy was contacted for comment.

In June, D’iu allegedly traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City, where his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who helped him cross the US-Mexico border. After entering the US, he was allegedly instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software to “facilitate his assignments”.

View image in fullscreen Igor D’iu’s allegedly falsified US passport. Photograph: US Department of JusticeD’iu’s co-conspirators also allegedly directed him to visit a cafe near the company’s Palo Alto office, identify employees and photograph their laptop screens as they worked. They further instructed him to “position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity”, the justice department said.

The alleged surveillance gradually expanded, with D’iu allegedly instructed to monitor employees and their residences. The justice department said he reportedly conducted online searches for multiple employees’ home addresses, including that of a senior executive.

In early September, D’iu allegedly followed a female employee in a silver Lexus SUV for nearly 30 miles (48km) as she drove from the company’s Palo Alto office toward San Francisco. According to the justice department, the employee repeatedly attempted to evade him, at one point driving into a grocery store parking lot.

Officials said D’iu “allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle”. The employee eventually called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco police department’s Mission station.

D’iu allegedly abandoned the pursuit after the employee contacted a police officer. The justice department added that investigators had also obtained evidence indicating he had followed other employees on previous occasions.

View image in fullscreen Igor D’iu’s Russian passport. Photograph: US Department of JusticeAfter Palo Alto police contacted D’iu about the alleged stalking incident, he reportedly changed vehicles and obtained a new phone number. His co-conspirators then allegedly instructed him to travel to Reno, Nevada, before he returned to the Bay Area to continue his assignments, the justice department said.

The justice department also accused D’iu of obtaining fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity. Investigators reportedly intercepted two international packages containing concealed ID documents, including a fake California ID card and an altered US passport. Officials said the passport was authentic and had originally been issued to another individual in the US before being modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

Investigators also discovered a social security card bearing the name “Hugo Landry Johns”. During an FBI search of D’iu’s East Palo Alto residence in October, investigators recovered approximately $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports, wireless networking equipment and additional fraudulent ID documents.

They also found a notebook containing 10 handwritten addresses, several of which belonged to the residences of company employees. The notebook also included detailed profiles of at least three employees, documenting their family members’ names, educational and employment histories, and an “assessment of their strengths and weaknesses”.

In response to the indictment, M Scott Proctor, acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, said: “The Americans who build our defense technology help keep this country safe by arming our warfighters with the tools and weapons they need to prevail against our adversaries and enemies.

“As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry. Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of US sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation,” he added.

news.title: U.S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.
news.title_en: U.S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.

news.author: Natasha Singer and Dana Goldstein
news.summary_en:
Three of the largest U.S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.

Starting next year, Google said, its A.I.-related products, including Search and its Gemini app, will be turned off automatically for schools, and administrators can choose to turn those A.I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available
news.article_content_en:
Three of the largest U.S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.

Starting next year, Google said, its A.I.-related products, including Search and its Gemini app, will be turned off automatically for schools, and administrators can choose to turn those A.I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available without A.I. chatbot features, meaning schools that want to forgo A.I. will lose access to an important learning tool.

Google’s approach created a firestorm of criticism from lawmakers, government officials, education leaders and parents, some of whom said the tech giant was trying to force its A.I. into public schools.

Now, some schools across the United States are blocking Google’s A.I. in search — or considering alternative providers.

“If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options,” Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement. “We refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out.”

Google’s new use-it-or-lose-it stance on A.I. in search underscores how the tech giant’s interlocking ecosystem of Chromebook laptops and apps like Gmail and Docs has become essential classroom infrastructure. The company’s search engine is a go-to product for teaching students how to do research and find primary sources.

But some educators worry that the generative A.I. that Google has embedded in its search engine for consumers could hinder students’ critical thinking, undermine learning and present safety risks. Some students have used the chatbots embedded in search to cheat, they have said, or scanned A.I.-generated search summaries instead of reading historical documents and news sources.

Educators are balancing those concerns with the reality that A.I. has already become an important tool in the work force, that a majority of U.S. teenagers already use chatbots and that many students will need to use A.I. in their future jobs.

Medical associations have also warned that developing relationships with chatbots could have negative mental health effects on young people. Earlier this month, two parents in North Carolina sued Google, saying their daughter had developed a plan to die by suicide after prolonged chats with the company’s A.I. on search on her school Chromebook. (Google said it had built safeguards into its A.I. features in search to help young people find emergency resources and was reviewing the claims in the lawsuit.)

Now districts like Chicago Public Schools, the fourth-largest U.S. school system, are urging Google to provide them with a version of search without A.I. features. “If such an arrangement can’t be reached,” Chicago Public Schools said in an email, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

Among the search engine alternatives for schools: DuckDuckGo and Microsoft’s Bing. Both offer options to disable A.I.-generated answers.

Google argued this month that it would be providing schools with more options to control student A.I. access — not fewer. Administrators could give students access to A.I. Mode, a chatbot-like function in search, as well as A.I. Overview, which summarizes search results, the company said. It is also pilot testing Guided Learning, a new chatbot widget intended to break down academic questions for students without providing easy answers.

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” Google said in a statement, noting that next year the company would turn off its Gemini app and search engine for schools “until schools decide which services to enable.”

Over the last three years, the company has made building generative A.I. a top business priority. And Google has integrated its Gemini A.I. chatbot throughout its software suite.

The fight over Google’s A.I. products has been brewing for months, with district leaders and teachers across the country approaching Google employees at meetings and online to request greater control over how students interact with generative A.I.

School tech directors in four states said they and their colleagues had repeatedly pressed Google this year to let schools decide which A.I. tools, if any, might be appropriate for students in different grades. And they warned that Google’s all-or-nothing approach to search essentially overrode more nuanced school policies on student A.I. use.

“We need to be able to control our own pace,” said Chris Warden, the technology director at Central R-3 School District in Park Hills, Mo., “not have Google tell us what the pace of A.I. adoption is going to be.”

In September, the New York City Department of Education and the Los Angeles Unified School District announced moratoriums on student use of generative A.I.

At the start of this school year, Google’s education team helped Los Angeles schools turn off A.I. mode for students logged into their school Google accounts, according to school board members. But Google said during its announcement this month that its A.I. features were so “deeply integrated” in search that it could not provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine.

Google’s decision prompted groups of parents to protest last week in front of the company’s Boston, Boulder, Chicago, New York and Portland offices.

In Chicago, several dozen parents and educators chanted slogans like, “Hey, Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini.”

“We don’t want corporations determining what is happening in our kids’ classrooms and how our schools are run,” said Cassie Creswell, the executive director of a parent group called Illinois Families for Public Schools, who helped organize the Chicago rally.

Parents and students also protested in Venice, Calif., carrying signs like “We don’t need Alphabet to teach the alphabet.”

At a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee two days later, Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, was applauded when he said, “We have choices” as to which company’s software to use. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight,” he added.

This week, Jenn Brown, a Google program manager, offered an explanation for the company’s refusal to provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine for students. Google now considers search to be fundamentally an A.I. product, she said during a monthly Google Meet for school tech leaders, according to a school administrator who attended the discussion.

New York City, Los Angeles and other school districts said they were using a combination of software controls and filters to independently block student access to A.I. in Google search. Even so, some New York City parents have found students can still easily access A.I. Mode at home when signed into their student Google accounts.

New York City has declined to participate in the pilot of Google’s new chatbot feature for students, according to the district. Instead, the district is conducting its own research of five other A.I. tools for potential use at the high-school level.

In the absence of A.I. controls from Google, some smaller school districts are also working to independently disable chatbots in search. In Missouri, Mr. Warden said his rural school district, which serves about 2,000 students, had signed up for a new service from Lightspeed Systems, an online student monitoring service for schools. The software is designed to block student access to A.I. Overview and A.I. Mode in Google search.

The backlash against Google has complicated some school districts’ plans to teach students how to use chatbots effectively, said Nick Melvoin, a Los Angeles school board member.

“Ironically, it undermines the goal of trying to get some A.I. into schools,” Mr. Melvoin said.

news.article_content_en:
According to Zhitong Finance APP, Anthropic (ANT.US) disclosed in a regulatory filing on Thursday that, as part of its initial public offering (IPO), the company raised approximately $300 million from Japanese investors. USD hundreds of millions, at the lower end of the planned fundraising range. The Japanese offering segment of this Claude chatbot developer sold 36.1 million shares of Class A at a price of $83 per share. The shares priced above the previously announced range. The number of shares sold was lower than the originally planned 38.5 million to 50 million; the Japanese portion was initially expected to raise $30 billion to $35 billion.

Japan is one of the few markets where retail buyers can directly participate in this IPO. This also provides much-needed support to Japan’s capital markets. Data shows that, as of 2026, With only about a month left until the end of the year, the amount raised through IPOs denominated in Japanese yen this year is currently lower than in any full year since 2011.

This artificial intelligence company and its seven co-founders raised a total of $107.3 billion in this scaled-up IPO and private placement. The company sold 956.4 million shares, and the co-founders sold 23.6 million shares.

news.title: At DealBook, Elon Musk says he feels "pretty foolish" after spending nearly $500M backing Republicans in midterms won by Democrats and claims "I'm not MAGA" (Todd Spangler/Variety)
news.title_en: At DealBook, Elon Musk says he feels "pretty foolish" after spending nearly $500M backing Republicans in midterms won by Democrats and claims "I'm not MAGA" (Todd Spangler/Variety)

inline_images.caption: Getty Images

news.author: Variety
news.content_snippet:
Elon Musk spent big backing Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections — which resulted in a sweeping defeat of the GOP as Democrats took over the House and Senate.

Musk spent nearly $500 million during the midterms, including $200 million to try to defeat Senator-elect James Talarico in Texas in his race against Lone Star State attorney general Ken Paxton.

Earlier at the conference, Skydance CEO David Ellison said Musk — whose roles include founder, CEO and chief engineer of SpaceX and CEO of
news.summary_en: Elon Musk admitted feeling 'foolish' for his $500M political donation to the GOP during the 2026 midterms, distancing himself from the MAGA movement. Additionally, Musk confirmed his investment in Skydance and revealed that SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a potential merger due to increasing operational synergies.

news.title: Gemini 4 Neon costs $3/1M input tokens and $15/1M output tokens; the model sits between Hydrogen and Carbon and replaces Argon in the Gemini app (Abner Li/9to5Google)
news.title_en: Gemini 4 Neon costs $3/1M input tokens and $15/1M output tokens; the model sits between Hydrogen and Carbon and replaces Argon in the Gemini app (Abner Li/9to5Google)
news.author: 9to5Google
news.content_snippet:
Following last week’s release of Carbon and Hydrogen, Google today is rolling out Gemini 4 Neon. The model offers “frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.”

Neon has performance comparable to, if not surpassing, Carbon across coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks, but at Flash speeds and a lower cost.

As such, Neon is available in the Gemini app for AI Pro (and AI Ultra) subscribers, with 3.1 Pro finally going away. Neon also replaces Argo
news.summary_en: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, a model designed to balance frontier-level reasoning with production efficiency, positioned between Hydrogen and Carbon. It features a 1M-token context window for coding and agentic tasks, priced at $3/1M input tokens and $15/1M output tokens.

news.title: Trump Administration Unveils Project to Combat Cybercrime
news.title_en: Trump Administration Unveils Project to Combat Cybercrime

inline_images.caption: Scott Patterson

news.author: Bloomberg
news.summary_en:
The Trump administration is launching a new effort to combat a surge in crypto fraud and other cybercrimes targeting Americans, attacks that largely come from criminal networks located overseas.

news.summary_en: Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks is acquiring AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion and has raised its FY2027 revenue guidance. The acquisition seeks to integrate AI infrastructure management with cybersecurity, mitigating risks associated with open-weight model deployment.
news.article_content_en:
A Palo Alto Networks logo is seen in this illustration taken August 18, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration

Nov 18 : Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and signed a deal to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in a deal valued at $4.5 billion, as a heightened threat environment pushes customers toward broader security products.

Shares of Palo Alto jumped about 10 per cent in after-hours trading to $368.60, and drove gains in rivals. CrowdStrike rose 5.3 per cent, Zscaler climbed 3 per cent and Fortinet gained 2.1 per cent.

Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi.

The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks, giving attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.

"As AI accelerates cyber attacks, enterprises are moving with urgency to replace disjointed tools with unified platforms," Palo Alto CEO Nikesh Arora said during the company's analyst call on Wednesday.

With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto is looking to offer users a technology platform to help customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI.

Open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released, present security challenges, including the risk of model tampering, data leakage and misuse by bad actors.

"Applied Compute extends Palo Alto's push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI. The opportunity is to bring AI infrastructure and security closer together," said Shaul Eyal, analyst at TD Cowen.

The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.

Palo Alto now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, compared with its prior expectation of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion.

Its first-quarter revenue came in at $3.45 billion, up 39 per cent from a year earlier, beating estimates of $3.31 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

news.article_content_en:
New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

news.title_en: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
news.author: Lauren Goode
news.summary_en:
Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.

Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s mo
news.article_content_en:
Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.

Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce. And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.”

By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it:

Tuesday’s earnings call:

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”

Wednesday’s all-hands meeting:

“Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.”

Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again:

Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together.

“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.”

Kress’ new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?)

Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment.

Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase, adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post.

And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot.

Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.

Paresh Dave contributed to this article.

Here, we look more closely at the expert-level design improvements behind the Jalapeño gains and how we’re applying the same approach to deliver significant gains on third-party hardware with AMD.

To measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings. And to ground capability development in trusted evaluators, we’re working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation (EDA) tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips.

### Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks

We started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as:

In the vector unit, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage.

In the matrix unit, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block.

Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up.

### Our collaboration with AMD

We have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions.

We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area.

AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline.

### Optimizing RISC-V cores

Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads.

We gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects.

We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero.

With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both.

### Designing a RISC-V core from a specification

For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task.

At about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

Starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. Requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design.

### What’s next

We have demonstrated that our models can explore new processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU. To ground model development in trusted evaluators and broaden the design challenges addressed, we’re partnering with Synopsys to train GPT‑Synopsys, a new model, to use Synopsys electronic design automation (EDA) tools the way expert chip designers do.

news.title_en: Even His Own Officials Don’t Think Trump’s China Trip Will Lead to Progress on AI
news.author: Hugo Lowell

news.summary_en: President Trump is set to meet with President Xi, yet the proposed AI incident hotline between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng remains non-operational. Friction is exacerbated by divergent threat assessments—US concerns over autonomous model misalignment versus China's focus on domestic stability—compounded by the intelligence scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
news.article_content_en:
Ahead of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping on Thursday, administration officials privately tell Inner Loop they see little room for progress in alleviating AI safety and espionage concerns.

As he departed the White House, Trump left it an open question whether he would press Xi on Chinese interference in AI or the Nvidia scandal, as part of what officials say is an effort to not antagonize China during the summit.

But the fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, has made any negotiations around AI development fraught for the world's two largest economies, officials say.

Back in September, the Trump administration moved to set up an AI incident hotline between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese vice premier He Lifeng to account for situations just like this one. Unfortunately, the communication channel remains at the concept stage and is not operational.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters last week the US and Chinese governments had engaged in AI safety talks at a “technical level” since the hotline announcement, but admitted it was “still a work in progress.”

Trump officials have previously discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.

Part of the reason progress hasn’t been made yet is due to differing views on what the biggest risks are with AI—and both nations have different incentives on making incidents public, officials say.

In the US, Trump administration officials and tech leaders have been most worried about AI models becoming autonomous and misaligned, where they can operate beyond the bounds of human oversight.

But in China, government officials are widely understood to be more concerned about advanced open-weight models being used by critics and dissidents inside the country to undermine the Chinese Communist Party, officials say.

In an added complication, the Chinese government has appeared interested in using frontier AI models to gather intelligence domestically and abroad, and would be unlikely to report situations where their models went rogue, officials say.

Suspicions about mutual espionage have also exacerbated the distrust on any AI-related negotiations, officials tell Inner Loop. China has viewed the US as trying to stymie its AI development—and that was even before the Nvidia scandal.

China has forcefully bristled at allegations that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese intelligence agency, calling them “groundless” and a “smear.”

While Trump has sought to forge friendlier economic relations with China, the administration this week announced it would move forward with a new rule clamping down on China's ability to remotely access US-made AI chips in foreign data centers.

It marked a direct intervention by Trump in response to the alleged role of Megaspeed in the Nvidia scandal and criticism that a firm with ties to China had gained access to advanced AI chips. The rule could also prevent similar companies that might have their corporate parents in China from doing business with Nvidia, WIRED has previously reported.

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

news.title_en: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways
news.author: Louise Matsakis
news.content_snippet:
This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China. This is known as remote access.

But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing
news.summary_en: The Trump administration has mandated special licensing for overseas data centers providing large-scale computing power to China, effectively closing the 'remote access' loophole. Additional export controls were imposed on Singapore and Malaysia to curb chip smuggling, a move triggered by the scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his ties to Chinese intelligence assets.
news.article_content_en:
This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China. This is known as remote access.

But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place.

These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life.

As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling.

The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”)

It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips.

It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations.

The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead.

Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week.

The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China.

At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter.

According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.)

Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips.

But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue?

For one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies.

Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China.

Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished.

There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult.

This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment.

The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources.

I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life.

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
paragraphs: This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China. This is known as remote access.

But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place.

These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life.

As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling.

The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”)

It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips.

It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations.

The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead.

Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week.

The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China.
At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter.

According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.)

Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips.

But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue?

For one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies.

Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China.
Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished.

There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult.

This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment.

The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources.

I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life.

news.article_content_en:
Google released Gemini 4 Neon, promising "frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows."The model is live today through the API at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, above Carbon and Argon's introductory rate of $2/$10 (doubling to $4/$20 on December 1) and twice the price of Hydrogen at $1.50/$7.50.

Neon offers a context window of about one million tokens and can produce up to one million output tokens. It handles text, images, video, audio, and PDFs, with support for Computer Use, code execution, file search, and grounding via Google Search and Maps. Image and audio generation aren't supported.

Full specs are in the documentation. Benchmarks should follow in the next few hours. If Carbon and Argon are Google's counterparts to OpenAI's Astra or Anthropic's Fable, Neon is likely its Claude Opus or Sol equivalent. It's also Google's fourth new Gemini 4 model in four weeks.

news.article_content_en:
President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.

Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.

"Peace and prosperity for whom?"

“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.

Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.

At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.

Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.

“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”

“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”

The agency says the project will be on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.

"There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here"

The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.

He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.

Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.

And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

news.article_content_en:
If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?

But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.

It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.

If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.

TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.

Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.

Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.

Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?

But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.

And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.

Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.

But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.

In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.

On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.

Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.

“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”

Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.

In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.

Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

news.title_en: Google Deepmind's Project Genie update brings Genie 4, chainable worlds, and a community gallery for remixing
news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.summary_en:
Google Deepmind is releasing Genie 4, its most advanced world model for generating interactive 3D worlds. The new version, previously available only as a research preview, is part of a major update to Project Genie and is now open to Google AI Ultra subscribers. Genie 4 lets users reshape worlds through text input in real time, changing weather, characters, or storylines. The model also generates native real-time sound that adapts to the scene.

The older Genie 3 is getting updates too: longer s
news.article_content_en:
Google Deepmind is releasing Genie 4, its most advanced world model for generating interactive 3D worlds. The new version, previously available only as a research preview, is part of a major update to Project Genie and is now open to Google AI Ultra subscribers. Genie 4 lets users reshape worlds through text input in real time, changing weather, characters, or storylines. The model also generates native real-time sound that adapts to the scene.

The older Genie 3 is getting updates too: longer sessions of up to three minutes, 360-degree panorama support, and chainable worlds. A new AI agent helps build worlds from spoken descriptions, and a community gallery lets users share and remix creations. All generated content carries SynthID watermarks and goes through safety checks. Google AI Pro members can join a waitlist.

news.title: Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
news.title_en: Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
news.author: Lauren Feiner
news.summary_en:
With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits.

news.article_content_en:
With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits.

On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against users who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.

“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a new bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.

“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”

Roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that users were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the company’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly big hammer.”

Roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a new Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.

Litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake issue through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a new wave of legal challenges.

“You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”

In addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”

The Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she said she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”

Hilton said over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”

Hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who said a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how quickly technology advances.”
